extracted.subtask_description: Qualitative study of how political leaders' tweets influence newspaper political journalists' coverage and what makes some tweets especially able to shape coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: generators of story ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets act as sources of story ideas by surfacing topics and conversations journalists might not otherwise see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants reported seeing tweets (e.g., about surveillance drones or local endorsements) that 'spark within me an idea' or 'add to the mix of things to eventually write about.' Use tweets from a wide range of actors to discover novel story leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: tip sheets for events that they might have otherwise missed
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets serve as alerting tools that tip journalists to events, press conferences, or happenings worth pursuing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: officials tweeting about legislative happenings or agency actions can 'tip us to something happening in the legislature.' Journalists sometimes 'pick up ideas, breaking news tips, even press statements from Twitter.'

rubrics_metrics.name: places to go to find quotes and polling data
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists use tweets as sources of quotable material and for rapid dissemination of polling/statistical information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include using a candidate's tweet as a direct quote (Ann Romney example) and following pollsters via Twitter because 'Twitter is exceptionally well-suited for getting out polling information.' Tweets that contain quotable, attributable lines are especially useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: ways to expand access to a wide range of sources to get alternative viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Following many political actors on Twitter gives journalists access to diverse perspectives they can incorporate into coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marc follows 'about 860 people: left, right, and center' to obtain different perspectives. Journalists consciously follow diverse accounts to avoid perceived bias and include alternative views in stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: forms of background information that help them better understand issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets and linked content provide background material that shapes journalists' understanding and framing of issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hashtags like #SSM helped a reporter filter discussion about same-sex marriage; links to reports can reveal non-intuitive angles (e.g., job loss in government sector). Such background may not appear verbatim in stories but guides coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: ways to double-check information in existing stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists use tweets to verify facts, reveal errors, or prompt corrections and tweaks to stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eddy noted that 'Twitter responses have caused me, and other reporters, to correct an error or make some other, generally minor, tweak to a story.' Use tweets as a rapid cross-checking resource.

rubrics_metrics.name: the breaking nature/timeliness of the information
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets that are timely or breaking are particularly valued for immediate reporting needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitter is called 'possibly the ultimate breaking news tool.' Speed and timeliness make tweets useful 'on deadline' for instant reactions (the 'first draft' of who said what).

rubrics_metrics.name: information that adds value to an existing story being worked on (topicality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets that supplement or add topical detail to an ongoing story are more likely to be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists look for tweets that are 'topical' or that provide 'nuggets of news' that 'add value to an existing story' (e.g., candidate outreach, fundraising totals). Such tweets fit well into stories currently under development.

rubrics_metrics.name: an insider's perspective on what is really going on politically
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets that convey an unvarnished, insider view or explain processes/events are especially useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists prize 'plainspoken and revealing' tweets or live, in-the-moment commentary (e.g., a politician tweeting committee-level insights). Such insider perspective can drive second-level agenda effects by emphasizing certain attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: information that quickly gets to the point (conciseness/readability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short, punchy, easy-to-read tweets attract journalists' attention and are more likely to be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robbie: 'I tend to focus on the ones that are short and punchy … with a quick sentence.' Tracie: 'to-the-point tweets stand out' given reporters' time pressures. Long or vague tweets are less useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: source type matters: bloggers, think tanks, and interest groups are often more useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets from political bloggers, think tanks, and interest groups tend to be rated higher by journalists than tweets from candidates or elected officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants said think tanks/interest groups 'are more about analyzing issues' and often link to in-depth analyses; bloggers can produce 'mini-scoops.' Candidates' tweets often 'read like a press release' and are less valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: use of hashtags to increase discoverability and group conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hashtags make tweets searchable and help spread views beyond followers, aiding journalists in locating relevant conversation clusters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hashtags (e.g., #p2, #tcot, #SSM) group tweets so journalists can search and filter discussion. Hashtags help political leaders 'spread their views beyond their followers' and let reporters 'filter out a lot of noise.'

rubrics_metrics.name: links to deeper analyses or reports increase utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets that link to substantive analyses, reports, or data are particularly valuable because they provide material suitable for newspaper analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think tanks tweeting links to analyses were described as 'sometimes useful' because the linked in-depth content better fits newspapers' emphasis on analysis rather than just reporting. Journalists follow links to find sources for interviews or background.

rubrics_metrics.name: perceived credibility and availability of other information affect tweet value
rubrics_metrics.description: The usefulness of a tweet (information subsidy) depends on who sent it and whether corroborating information is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information subsidies 'vary in value depending on the perceived credibility of the source and the availability of other information.' Journalists must check veracity and methodology when tweets link to partisan reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: tweets as instant reactions or 'first draft' comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets are used to capture immediate reactions from political players and to populate early story drafts with attributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sydney: Twitter has become the 'first draft of the '...said in a statement' comment'—useful for rapid attribution of reactions after events like court decisions. These often serve as immediate color or reaction material.
